chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
title: Writing the baritone with the bass in arrangements
summary: Durham sometimes wrote the baritone with the bass, as in Lunceford's band and Running a Temperature, for heavy reed tone in the bass section.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So I wrote a little of that with different bands at times, you know. That's why we used to -- a lot of arrangers, way back, when they had a baritone,
like Lunafords band, a lot of times I wrote the bass -- baritone with the bass. You didn't even know it, saxes going nowhere and the baritone, he's going with the bass.
Yeah, I think you can hear that on some of the records.
Yeah. We didn't make it distinctive, just solely bass all the time. But I'd move into that bass with the baritone, sustain it, yeah.
Would it give it a sort of -- now, what --
Give it a heavy reed tone in that bass section.
Yeah, but it takes away from the sax section.
No, it didn't bother the sax section.
This was when they had five saxes, or four?
Four.
And you put the baritone playing with the bass?
Sometimes, in some spots, like Running A Temperature. If you listen close, the baritone is going out in a direction away from the other saxes all together. In Running A Temperature.
Well, I can tell where that would sound
The baritone carries.
Yeah.
It carries.
Carried more than the bass?
Yeah, more than the other saxes.
Well, you felt the bass, but you didn't hear it very often.
Yeah, baritone carries heavy.
Yeah.
Carries a lot of volume.
That was really a good idea, because --
I know -- quite a few bands out West now that are doing it. Not all the time, but they'll find a place where they play bass with that baritone, staccato bass, you know.
